nameStory: Bog wintergreen gets its name from its favorite wet, boggy homes and its remarkable ability to stay green all winter long. While most plants lose their leaves or turn brown in the cold, this tough little member of the heath family keeps its glossy leaves bright green under the snow, earning it the 'wintergreen' name shared with its close relatives.
description: Bog wintergreen is a small, low-growing perennial herb that hugs the ground in wet, acidic places. It forms small patches of glossy, rounded leaves that stay green year-round, rising only 3-6 inches tall. In summer, it sends up delicate stalks topped with nodding pink or white bell-shaped flowers that look like tiny lanterns. This quiet woodland gem is much less common than its wintergreen cousins in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pink to white bell-shaped flowers nod downward from a single stalk, each flower about the size of a small pea with 5 rounded petals that curve backward, blooming June through August

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, glossy, heart-shaped to kidney-shaped leaves feel almost waxy to the touch and remain bright green through winter, growing in a basal rosette close to the ground

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low patches 3-6 inches tall, spreading slowly by underground stems called rhizomes, often growing in small colonies in boggy areas

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny seeds that are so light they look like dust when shaken from the pod

habitat: Look for bog wintergreen in wet, acidic soils of sphagnum bogs, cedar swamps, and soggy woodland edges, especially where the ground stays consistently moist. In New England, it's quite rare and typically found in cooler, northern areas with other bog-loving plants like pitcher plants and cranberries. It prefers partially shaded spots where the soil has that characteristic spongy, peaty feel of wetland areas.

seasonality.spring: New flower stalks begin emerging from the center of leaf rosettes in late spring, while last year's glossy green leaves remain prominent and easy to spot.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August with distinctive nodding pink or white bell flowers, making this the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules ripen, while the evergreen leaves remain glossy and green, beginning their winter persistence phase.
seasonality.winter: The thick, waxy leaves stay bright green under snow, making this one of the few native plants you can identify by its persistent foliage in the coldest months.

funFact: Despite being called 'wintergreen,' bog wintergreen doesn't actually contain the minty wintergreen oil that gives wintergreen gum and candy their flavor - that comes from a completely different plant family, making this one of botany's most misleading common names!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative shinleaf wintergreen, but bog wintergreen has more kidney-shaped leaves and prefers much wetter habitats. Remember: if your feet are getting wet and the leaves look like little hearts or kidneys, you've probably found bog wintergreen rather than the oval-leaved shinleaf.
contextualKnowledge: The wintergreen name causes endless confusion because true wintergreen flavor comes from birch trees and a completely different plant called eastern teaberry, neither of which are related to the Pyrola wintergreens. These Pyrola species got the wintergreen name purely for their evergreen leaves, not for any minty properties.
compareHints: Among New England's Pyrola species, bog wintergreen stands out for its heart-shaped to kidney-shaped leaves and preference for very wet habitats. Shinleaf has oval leaves and grows in drier woods, while American wintergreen has more pointed leaves with visible veins. The pink flowers and boggy habitat make bog wintergreen the easiest to distinguish once you know where to look.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American wintergreen stands out from its Pyrola cousins by having the largest, thickest leaves with the most prominent white veining.

Among the New England wintergreens, shinleaf stands out with its distinctly oval (elliptical) leaves - American wintergreen has more rounded leaves, while green-flowered wintergreen has greenish flowers instead of white.
Among the wintergreen genus, green-flowered wintergreen is the only one with distinctly greenish flowers - American wintergreen, shinleaf, and bog wintergreen all have white to pinkish blooms.
Among New England's wintergreens, lesser wintergreen is the smallest with the roundest leaves - shinleaf has larger oval leaves, while American wintergreen has more pointed leaves with visible veins.
